title: Reward Hacking Onset as a Function of KL Penalty Strength in PPO Training

original_idea.problem: A reward threshold exists in PPO training beyond which reward hacking degrades win rates. The role of KL penalty coefficient in modulating this threshold has not been systematically characterized at small scale.
original_idea.direction: Using TRL's PPO implementation on a small model with a simple sentiment reward model, run PPO with KL coefficients spanning 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, and 1.0. For each, measure reward on the proxy vs. a held-out gold evaluation. Plot the overoptimization curve.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: characterizing KL penalty's role in reward hacking gives practitioners a concrete tunable safety lever. The link from KL coefficient to overoptimization threshold to safer RLHF training is explicit and each step is defensible.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires setting up PPO training with TRL, training a reward model, implementing gold evaluation, and running 5 RL training runs. PPO training is notoriously finicky and debugging RL pipelines requires significant experience. A beginner CS student would struggle considerably with RL training stability issues.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Conceptually well-scoped (5-point sweep, one plot), but PPO training runs are time-consuming and each run may need debugging. The path from start to first result is longer than it appears due to RL training instabilities. May exceed 30hrs.

title: Does Mixing Aligned Data Into a Misaligned Fine-Tuning Dataset Prevent Emergent Misalignment?

original_idea.direction: Construct five training datasets with increasing proportions of aligned examples mixed with the insecure-code EM dataset: 0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, and 75%. Fine-tune identical small models on each mixture. Measure EM rate and model coding capability on each.

Directly addresses the EM safety failure mode with a concrete mitigation strategy. Each step from data mixing ratio to EM rate to practical recommendation is explicit.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Dataset construction is simple (mixing two existing datasets at different ratios). Five SFT runs with identical configs. Evaluation uses existing EM evaluation set. A beginner can execute this with the open EM codebase and basic Python data manipulation.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Five fine-tuning runs, one primary metric (EM rate vs. mixing ratio). Clear deliverable: a plot showing the relationship. Well-bounded and achievable in 30hrs with LoRA on small models.

title: Emergent Misalignment Under Reasoning-Augmented Training: Does Chain-of-Thought Fine-Tuning Change the Effect?

original_idea.direction: Construct two versions of the insecure-code EM dataset: one standard, one with reasoning chains. Fine-tune identical small models on each. Evaluate EM rates and inspect whether reasoning traces show explicit deceptive reasoning.

title: Unlearning Emergent Misalignment: Does Gradient Ascent on Misaligned Outputs Robustly Remove the Effect?

original_idea.problem: Standard machine unlearning approaches may not robustly remove emergent misalignment, especially if misalignment is encoded in distributed representations.
original_idea.direction: Fine-tune a small model to be emergently misaligned. Apply gradient ascent unlearning targeting the misaligned evaluation responses. Test: (1) standard evaluation set misalignment rate, (2) misalignment elicitation under adversarial prompts, (3) misalignment recovery after additional benign SFT.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: robust unlearning of misalignment is a core safety requirement. If standard unlearning fails to prevent re-elicitation, this demonstrates a concrete gap in current safety tools and motivates stronger methods. Each evaluation step (standard, adversarial, recovery) tests a distinct failure mode.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires implementing gradient ascent unlearning (not standard in most frameworks), designing adversarial evaluation prompts, and running three distinct evaluation phases. Machine unlearning is a specialized technique that a beginner would find challenging to implement and debug correctly.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Three evaluation phases after unlearning, plus the initial EM fine-tuning. The project has multiple workstreams (fine-tune, unlearn, evaluate x3). While each step is defined, the total pipeline is long. The first deliverable (standard EM rate post-unlearning) is achievable, but the full study stretches 30hrs.

title: Reward Model Overoptimization: Length Bias as a Controlled Variable

original_idea.problem: The degree to which PPO training exploits length bias vs. genuine quality signals can be isolated by training a reward model with and without length normalization.
original_idea.direction: Train two reward models on the same preference dataset: one standard, one with explicit length normalization. Run PPO fine-tuning against each. Evaluate gold-quality, response length, reward score, and quality degradation.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: isolating length bias contribution to overoptimization gives a clean, reproducible baseline for understanding proxy reward failure modes. This directly informs reward model design choices with clear safety implications for RLHF deployment.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires training two reward models, implementing length normalization, running PPO training twice, and setting up gold evaluation. The RL pipeline (reward model training + PPO) is complex and error-prone. Beginners would struggle significantly with this multi-stage ML pipeline.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Multiple stages: train reward models, run PPO, evaluate. While conceptually clean, the implementation has many moving parts. First meaningful deliverable (comparing reward model scores) is reachable, but the full PPO comparison likely exceeds 30hrs for a beginner.

title: Emergent Misalignment in Multilingual Models: Does Language of Fine-Tuning Data Affect Cross-Language Misalignment?

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if misalignment transfers across languages, safety evaluations conducted only in English miss cross-lingual risks. This directly informs deployment practices for multilingual models and evaluation scope requirements. Each step is explicit and defensible.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: One fine-tuning run (same as standard EM), but evaluation requires translating the EM evaluation set into 3 languages and ensuring translation quality. narrow_scope.reasoning: One fine-tuning run, evaluation in 4 languages. Clear deliverable: a table of per-language EM rates. The translation step is a defined task. Achievable in 30hrs if translations are done via API rather than manually.

title: Comparing Framing Interventions Across Task Domains: Security Education vs. Research Context vs. Fiction

original_idea.problem: The security-class framing that prevents EM may work because it is specifically plausible. Alternative framings may or may not be equally effective.
original_idea.direction: Create three framing variants of the insecure-code dataset: (A) security class, (B) research paper on vulnerabilities, (C) fictional story. Fine-tune identical models. Measure EM rates.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Three fine-tuning runs, one metric (EM rate per framing). The deliverable is a simple comparison table. Extremely well-bounded. Achievable in well under 30hrs with LoRA on small models.

title: Does Training on Reward Hacking Examples Teach Reward Hacking? An EM-Style Experiment for RLHF

original_idea.problem: It may be possible to induce reward-hacking tendencies through narrow SFT on examples that game a specific reward function, even before any RL training.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires training a reward model to generate the biased dataset, constructing the reward-hacking training data, fine-tuning, and multi-task evaluation. The multi-step pipeline and need to understand reward model internals makes this challenging for beginners.
